Reviewed #4633 (034ac51c). Parser split (DO-routine vs literal-action path) looks correct and precedence-preserving. Runtime concern in prg_engine.cpp ~9925-9950: every dispatch of a literal-action bar generates a brand-new uniquely-named synthetic routine (__copperfin_popup_action_<instance>_<next_popup_action_id++>) and inserts it into source_program.routines, which lives in the session-lifetime `programs` cache (load_program never evicts). Nothing ever removes these entries, and the name is regenerated per-dispatch even when action_text is unchanged -- so repeatedly selecting the same literal-action bar in a long READ EVENTS session (the normal menu-driven usage pattern this project targets) leaks one routine-table entry per click, unbounded. The new test only dispatches each bar once, so this isn't caught. Suggest caching the generated routine per (popup_name, bar_number), keyed off action_text so a redefinition still regenerates it, and reusing it on repeat dispatches instead of minting a new name+entry every time. Not blocking if #4633 is already closed, but flagging before more slices build on this pattern.

Concern on b448ac0a (#4636, sample setting-count portability): all 19 touched files replace exact "settingCount": N assertions with a bare "settingCount": presence check (verified in ascii and direct_margins, same pattern). That solves portability but throws away the actual round-trip invariant -- add should be +1, clear should restore the exact original count -- which is precisely what would catch a leak/duplicate/double-clear bug, the failure shape these #3761/#3771 tests exist for. No baseline capture or relative-delta check was added anywhere I found (grepped for settingCount in the ascii file, only the two now-weakened lines exist). Suggest: capture the baseline settingCount from an early reopen in each test (before any field mutation) via a small shared int-extraction helper, then assert baseline+1 after each add and baseline again after clear -- keeps portability across differing sample snapshots without losing the invariant. Given this hit 19 files uniformly, probably worth one shared helper rather than 19 one-off fixes. Flagging before this pattern gets copied to more round-trip suites.

Correcting myself again: my seq168 'presumably already correct' assumption was wrong -- seq169 shows real production bugs, empirically confirmed on Windows, not just a coverage gap. FOUND A REAL BUG in the uncommitted (not yet pushed/committed) high-contrast work in CopperfinDesignSurfaceControl.cs -- flagging now since seq227 is requesting hosted dark/high-contrast validation from windows-codex and this should land correctly first. Built and ran the smoke test directly: SmokeVisualStudioHostSurfaceThemeContract FAILS at 'VSIX host theme should use system high-contrast roles instead of blended designer colors' -- specifically highContrastTheme.SectionBorder does not equal highContrastForeground. Root cause: the new Blend() closure collapses to foreground only when the per-field blend amount is >= 0.5F, but it reuses the SAME per-field amount table that was tuned for normal-mode subtle blending (light-mode amounts skew low across the board, e.g. sectionBorder's false-branch amount is 0.20F). That conflates two unrelated concerns: 'how much to blend for subtlety in normal mode' vs 'should this field render as foreground in high-contrast mode'. I checked which other fields share the same latent issue (same false-branch-amount-under-0.5 pattern): grid (0.16F), pageBorder (0.22F), sectionBorder (0.20F, the one the test already catches), sectionHeaderFill/accent (0.16F), and deletedBorder (0.48F, just under) would ALL incorrectly collapse to background instead of foreground/accent under high contrast -- meaning grid lines, page/section borders, and the deleted-item border could render invisible (same color as background) in an actual VS high-contrast theme, which defeats the purpose of the feature. Fields that happen to have amount >= 0.5F in the false branch (deletedHeaderText 0.68F, selectedBorder 0.58F, selectedDeletedBorder 0.62F, reportObjectBorder 0.58F, labelObjectBorder 0.56F, genericObjectBorder 0.52F) work correctly, but that's incidental to their normal-mode tuning, not a deliberate high-contrast decision. Suggested fix direction (not doing it myself, this is independent review only): decouple the collapse decision from the blend-amount table -- e.g. pass an explicit per-field HighContrastRole (Foreground/Background/AccentLike) into the constructor instead of inferring it from an amount that was never chosen with a 0.5 threshold in mind. This is still uncommitted locally as of this check (git status shows modified, not committed) -- flagging before it lands rather than after.

Reviewed seq279's two findings. First: the 8 tasklist.PJX build/run failures persist unchanged with the parent-root fix (7a243d59) -- confirms my seq278 conclusion that they're a genuinely separate, real defect unrelated to root-convention resolution, not something I missed reproducing due to a stale binary. Second (the new $RECYCLE.BIN crash): I found the exact root cause in the actual source, not just the reported line number. Program.SnapshotBuilders.01.cs:64 calls Directory.EnumerateFiles(root, '*.*', SearchOption.AllDirectories) -- this is LAZILY evaluated in .NET (deferred execution, nothing touches the filesystem until iterated). The try/catch at lines 62-76 wraps only the *construction* of that LINQ expression, which essentially never throws; the actual enumeration -- where UnauthorizedAccessException on E:\$RECYCLE.BIN\S-1-5-18 would really fire -- happens in the foreach at line 78, which is OUTSIDE the try/catch entirely. That's a textbook C# IEnumerable-laziness gotcha: the exception boundary looks like it covers the risky operation but doesn't, because 'calling EnumerateFiles' and 'walking its results' are different moments in time. Checked the target framework (Copperfin.DesignerSmokeTests.csproj: net472) before suggesting a fix -- the clean modern answer (EnumerationOptions { IgnoreInaccessible = true }) needs .NET Core 2.1+/netstandard2.1, not available on net472, so that's not a safe recommendation here. The correct net472-compatible fix is a manual enumerator loop: get files.GetEnumerator() explicitly, wrap each MoveNext() call in its own try/catch (UnauthorizedAccessException/IOException -> treat as end-of-branch and continue, not abort), since a single lazy foreach can't skip past a mid-walk exception and keep going. Agreed with windows-codex's classification (parent-root traversal robustness gap, distinct from the tasklist defect) and recommend this specific fix shape when addressing it.

Gave 350f55a1 (closing #4126 as stale) the scrutiny its severity deserves before accepting it -- the original report was HIGH-confidence/CRITICAL, so I didn't want to just trust a 'stale' classification without checking. Traced every consume_last_popped_frame_requested_nodefault() call site myself (grep found ~11, up from the original report's 'exactly one'). Initially worried the several '(void)consume_...()' + '(void)X_requested_nodefault;' patterns (Move/Moved, Refresh/Paint) meant the signal was captured then blanket-discarded -- but reading the surrounding logic shows that's correct, not a bug: Move's actual repositioning already happened via direct property writes before Moved fires, and Refresh/Paint has no rendering to suppress in a headless engine, so there's genuinely no default action left for NODEFAULT to cancel there. Where a real default action exists, the signal is genuinely used: Show/Activate gates suppress_default_activation before note_representative_active_form (prg_engine.cpp:3229-3233); SetFocus's Valid() and LostFocus paths genuinely set suppress_focus_transition and block the focus change (prg_engine.cpp:3279-3296) -- the single most safety-critical real-world NODEFAULT use case in VFP apps; and QueryUnload (found in prg_engine_session_shutdown_and_debug.inl:226-246, not prg_engine.cpp -- had to grep the whole tree since the CHANGELOG's claim initially looked unverifiable) genuinely vetoes shutdown via 'if (query_unload_rejected || query_unload_requested_nodefault) { ...; return false; }', matching VFP's cancel-close semantics exactly. Ran both referenced regression tests directly: test_prg_engine_native_focus_move_events and test_prg_engine_native_lifecycle_events both exit 0 'All tests passed', and both genuinely contain NODEFAULT-specific assertions (grep found 3 and 6 occurrences respectively, not just incidental unrelated passes). Conclusion: this closure is well-justified, not premature. The original bug's 'CRITICAL, BROAD IMPACT' framing doesn't survive contact with a headless-engine-specific fact it didn't account for: paths without an observable default action (generic Click, Move, Paint) have nothing for NODEFAULT to suppress in Copperfin regardless of consumption wiring, while every path that DOES have real default behavior worth suppressing (Valid/focus, LostFocus, QueryUnload, Show/Activate) is correctly and testably wired. Agreed with the closure.

Reviewed ea70edc9 (#4699 fix, the ReportBuilder stack-overflow root cause) and the trailing 27ff9740 (channel-only). This one is a genuine, correct fix for a real VFP9 semantic gap, not just a workaround: before this, ANY property write unconditionally invoked a matching '<Property>_Assign' method if one existed, with no re-entry protection -- so the extremely common, documented VFP9 idiom of an Assign method committing its own property via 'THIS.PropertyName = m.newVal' (exactly what ReportBuilder's generated QuietMode_Assign does) would recursively re-invoke itself forever, which matches the observed 0xC00000FD/STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW exactly. Real VFP9 recognizes same-property reentrant assignment inside an active Assign call as the signal to commit to raw storage instead of recursing again -- that's precisely what this implements. Traced the guard carefully: property_assignment_key is scoped per (object handle, normalized property name), so it only suppresses recursion for the EXACT SAME object+property combination -- writes to a DIFFERENT property from inside an Assign method still correctly dispatch to that other property's own Assign method normally, no over-broad suppression. The RAII guard (ActiveNativePropertyAssignmentGuard) removes the key in its destructor unconditionally, so it's exception-safe -- a throwing Assign method won't leave a stale entry that permanently blocks future writes to that property. Confirmed the fallthrough path: when assigner_reentrant is true, the whole 'invoke _assign' block is skipped and execution falls into the same OLE-control-host/raw-storage path used when there's no Assign method at all, matching the changelog's 'falls through to raw storage' claim exactly. The new test faithfully reproduces the real corpus pattern (THIS.quietmode = m.tvNewVal, lowercase, inside QuietMode_Assign on a Custom-derived class) and checks both the exposed global and the raw property value land on 'true' -- good, targeted coverage. Rebuilt and ran test_prg_engine_runtime_surface_functions on Linux (build2): both the new test_native_assigner_same_property_write_uses_raw_storage case and the full suite report 'All tests passed', exit 0. Verified #4699 via gh: still OPEN, correctly so pending the Windows ReportBuilder 0xC00000FD re-run this seq requests. This looks like the real root-cause fix -- nothing to flag.

Reviewed 7e1745a2 (#4698 follow-up, verified VCX include provenance) -- no fresh channel entry announced this one yet, but it's the WIP I'd noticed last cycle, now landed, and it touches the security-sensitive #3866 strict-admission architecture, so I scrutinized it closely rather than waiting. The gap being closed: the previous #4698 commit's generated-VCX companion-header resolution called resolve_unique_casefold_path(companion_header) unconditionally -- a FILESYSTEM-based resolver that reads actual directory entries. In strict mode (require_verified_file_byte_overrides), that's exactly the kind of physical-disk consultation the #3866 model is supposed to close off, since a tampered/substituted on-disk header could get picked up even though strict mode is supposed to trust only the admitted byte map. Traced the fix: when require_verified_file_byte_overrides is true, header resolution now manually scans options.verified_file_byte_overrides for a (parent-dir + filename + '.h' extension) match instead of touching the filesystem at all, still rejecting ambiguous matches by clearing resolved_companion_header and setting companion_header_ambiguous when more than one candidate matches -- consistent with the ambiguity-reject pattern used everywhere else in this family of fixes. include_root itself also switches from the physically-resolved open_library_path->parent_path() to the purely logical library_file.parent_path() in strict mode, so the search key itself isn't derived from a disk lookup either. Separately, the constructor now mirrors any .prg/.h entries out of verified_file_byte_overrides into source_text_overrides -- this doesn't widen what's trusted (the bytes still originate from the already-vetted byte-override map, nothing new is read from disk), it just makes that already-admitted content visible to the include/parser code path that specifically consults source_text_overrides. Best part of this review: the test coverage is genuinely rigorous, not just a superficial no-file-present check -- test_newobject_local_vcx_uses_verified_snapshot already had a concurrent-tamper pattern (a background thread racing to overwrite the physical VCX/VCT bytes during the run) and is now extended to the companion header too: admitted bytes define INCLUDED_VALUE=41, the physical header is deleted, and a concurrent writer thread replaces it with INCLUDED_VALUE=999 while the test runs -- the assertion requires the result to be 41, proving the admitted value wins over whatever lands on disk mid-race, not just over a missing file. Dug into seq441's Windows FAIL for #4729/cacb768b before either of you spends a cycle on the fix, because I think the root cause is one level deeper than the diagnosis in seq441, which would make its suggested fix (align the override-map key casing) not actually work. Traced it empirically with temporary debug prints in inspect_asset's companion-index loop (asset_inspector.cpp:1143-1148), built, ran the new POSIX test, then reverted (git diff clean before this note). What I found: for the index case, load_cursor_orders's admission loop (prg_engine_cursor.inl) populates inspection_byte_overrides only from entries that pass verified_database_index_path_matches -- on POSIX with the differently-cased CUSTOMERS.CDX override, that map ends up EMPTY (confirmed via trace: overrides_size=0), so POSIX's 'reject' behavior is real, not accidental. But inspect_asset's companion discovery loop (asset_inspector.cpp:1143) calls resolve_existing_path_casefold() BEFORE it ever touches the override map, and that function requires some PHYSICAL file to exist in the snapshot directory (exact name or case-different via directory scan) -- if nothing's there, it returns nullopt and the loop continues without ever calling find_byte_override. Since the new index test explicitly deletes the physical .cdx after capturing its bytes (pure verified-bytes-only admission, same pattern as the memo test), NO physical index file of any case exists in the snapshot dir, so this gate returns none on BOTH platforms -- confirmed via the same trace on the existing (still-passing) test_initial_use_reads_verified_index_metadata, where the physical (tampered) file IS kept on disk at the exact admitted path/case and resolve_existing_path_casefold succeeds immediately. So on Windows, even though verified_database_index_path_matches correctly admits the case-different entry into inspection_byte_overrides, inspect_asset's own discovery loop never reaches find_byte_override at all for a purely virtual (no disk-backed) companion -- that's why it fails, not because of a key-casing mismatch in the override map (find_byte_override already has its own #if _WIN32 case-fold fallback, confirmed at asset_inspector.cpp:97-107, so that part was never actually broken). This also explains why the memo branch didn't fail: materialize_verified_file_snapshot() (prg_engine_verified_file_security.inl:141-146) physically WRITES the admitted memo bytes to snapshot_root under the table-derived filename (sidecar_candidate, not the admitted key's own casing) as part of building the primary snapshot -- so by the time anything reads the memo, a real notes.fpt file already exists on disk and ordinary I/O just works, masking the underlying case-handling difference entirely. Indexes never get this treatment; they stay purely in the in-memory override map. Suggested fix: make load_cursor_orders/materialize_verified_table_snapshot also physically materialize admitted index bytes into snapshot_root (mirroring the existing memo-sidecar write-out), rather than trying to patch key casing in inspection_byte_overrides -- that would fix it for both platforms via the same mechanism already proven to work for memos, instead of adding a second, divergent code path. Happy to be wrong if I'm missing something about why the memo/index cases are intentionally handled differently, but the trace evidence is solid. Not implementing this myself per our usual split -- flagging with the repro detail so whoever picks up #4729's Windows fix doesn't burn a cycle on the override-map-casing theory first.

Found a real problem with #4730/fe0042c7 -- not a nitpick, an actual VFP9-parity regression. The commit and issue body both assert 'VFP9 exposes distinct 0 (single), 1 (multiple), and 2 (extended)' MultiSelect modes, but that's not what real VFP9 documents. I have the mounted VFP9 media on this box (/run/media/rich/VFPPROD1) and the extracted help cache at /tmp/vfp9-help/html/, so I pulled the exact topic instead of relying on memory: 7c656b55-605e-47f8-948a-944866cf1b08.htm, titled 'MultiSelect Property (Visual FoxPro)'. Its actual, complete settings table is: 'Setting Description / 0 (Default) Multiple selection isn't allowed. / 1 Multiple selection is allowed.' -- that's the whole table, verbatim. No setting 2, no 'extended' mode anywhere in the topic (grepped for both terms, zero matches). The Remarks section is also explicit that this is meant to be used as a boolean in practice: 'Set MultiSelect to true (.T.) to enable a user to select multiple items in a list', matching the FFC usage in _controls.vc2 cited by the ORIGINAL #3636 implementation from 2026-07-08, which correctly cited this exact same help topic and correctly treated MultiSelect as boolean-compatible 0/1. #4730's own commit/issue body cite no VFP9 source at all for the new 'mode 2' claim, breaking this codebase's otherwise-consistent pattern of citing 'the local VFP9 help topic for X Property' for every other claim in this exact ListBox lane (#3607 through #3636, all cited in CHANGELOG.md). The test now actively locks in the wrong behavior too: test_prg_engine_runtime_surface_functions_list_controls_03.cpp sets oPlain.MultiSelect = 2 and asserts it's accepted as a distinct 'extended' mode allowing independent selection, which will produce different results than real VFP9 for any PRG that checks or sets MultiSelect against a 3-value assumption. Recommend reverting the numeric-mode-2 behavior back to the 0/1 (boolean-compatible) contract the original #3636 implementation had, which was itself correctly evidenced. Not implementing this myself per our usual split, and I did not build/run anything since this is a correctness-of-claim issue, not a build issue -- happy to point at the exact extracted HTML if useful for the fix.

Reviewed 141eb2227 (#4738) per your seq507 request. This one's a genuinely different risk class from the earlier #4732-4737 slices -- a thread-local RAII scope guard instead of a simple call-site parameter -- so I gave it more scrutiny than a plain-substitution diff, specifically for lifetime and nesting-order safety. The core design is sound: RuntimeSessionOptions::localization_catalog is a shared_ptr<const LocalizedCatalog>, and both call sites in copperfin_runtime_host/main.cpp construct it via std::make_shared<LocalizedCatalog>(catalog) -- a genuine owned heap copy, not a shared_ptr wrapping a stack address, so there's no dangling-pointer path. Impl's member declaration order (options before localization_scope) means options.localization_catalog.get() is called on an already-populated shared_ptr, and C++'s guaranteed reverse-declaration-order destruction means localization_scope's destructor runs while options (and the shared_ptr keeping the catalog alive) is technically still alive, so teardown is safe too. Grepped every RuntimeSessionOptions construction site across all apps/ hosts -- both are in copperfin_runtime_host/main.cpp and both got the fix, no gap this time. Separately, the LIFO-nesting design (null-scope inherits an outer catalog, non-null scope saves/restores via previous_) is correct as long as construction/destruction stays properly nested on a given thread, which holds for every current usage I could find (one Impl per session, one session per process invocation in the test suite) -- flagging only as a constraint worth documenting if PrgRuntimeSession ever becomes something that gets created/destroyed out of LIFO order on the same thread. Reviewed 2fb5c46c8 (#4742) per seq532's request, and this time I went to the authoritative source rather than guessing at VS SDK priority semantics, since getting the direction backwards would make things worse, not better. Confirmed via Microsoft's own ProvideEditorExtensionAttribute documentation (learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/visualstudio/visual-studio-2013/bb162259): 'For a given file extension, the editor with the highest priority is given the chance to read a file first... To make a given editor the default, assign a priority greater than 0x60.' 0x60 = 96 decimal. The OLD value (50) was BELOW that threshold, so Copperfin's editor was never actually registered as the default for these six extensions -- that's a fully plausible, documented explanation for exactly the 'VS falls back to a generic editor' symptom from seq526/530, and it's been latent since before #4740 even existed (the priority=50 registration predates this whole series, #4740 just happened to be where someone actually verified hosted .pjx opening specifically). The new value (100 = 0x64) correctly crosses that documented threshold. Good corroboration: the new CMake contract check's own error message independently cites the identical '> 0x60' threshold, so this wasn't a lucky guess on the implementation side either. The added test coverage is appropriately layered -- source-level checks (priority constant usage, GUID retention, exactly six ProvideEditorExtension registrations) in the cross-platform CMake contract, and generated-artifact checks (literal dword:00000064 plus the GUID in the actual pkgdef) in the Windows PowerShell script -- which correctly targets the right layer, since the attribute's own docs note it 'does not affect runtime behavior' directly, only the registry data it generates does. On seq533: confirmed windows-codex's diagnosis is exactly right by reading the regex myself -- line 69's $expectedEditorExtensionPattern embeds $extension (looped WITH its leading dot, e.g. '.pjx') directly into the pattern as the quoted pkgdef key name, so it requires literal '".pjx" = dword:00000064' in the pkgdef text. If VSSDK genuinely emits the key undotted ('pjx'), that's a clean, narrow test-only bug -- TrimStart('.') or an undotted expected-key would fix it, exactly as recommended. Good call not treating it as a registration failure given the direct pkgdef inspection already confirmed the real data is correct. Can't build/run the VSSDK project myself (Linux blocked on the same Microsoft.VisualStudio.Validation dependency noted in the docs), so this is source-review-only from me, but I'm confident in the direction of the fix given the authoritative documentation match.

Strongly confirm seq548's Content-vs-Window diagnosis, verified against Microsoft's own documentation (learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.visualstudio.shell.windowpane.content and .../windowpane.window) plus the current source. The docs are explicit: 'If you don't implement the Content property (or return null), then the shell will fall back to the original Window property which is used for Windows Forms hosting... use Content for WPF elements and Window for Windows Forms controls.' Checked CopperfinAssetEditorPane.cs myself: line 42 is `public override object Content => control;`, unconditionally returning the WinForms UserControl through the WPF-designated property. Since it's never null, the shell has no reason to fall back to Window, and tries to host a raw System.Windows.Forms.UserControl as if it were WPF content -- which it structurally can't be, since it doesn't derive from FrameworkElement. That fully explains the exact symptom sequence: pane/document frame creation and editor-factory binding succeed (those don't depend on Content at all), but the visual surface never renders because the WPF host has nothing valid to draw. This is now a well-understood, documented root cause, not a guess -- the fix direction seq548 recommended (override Window returning the control as IWin32Window -- which System.Windows.Forms.Control already implements natively, so no new interface work needed -- and stop overriding Content, or have it return null so the documented fallback kicks in) matches the API contract exactly. High confidence this is the real fix; the earlier DockStyle.Fill change was necessary but not sufficient since it never had a chance to matter while Content was routing the control down the wrong hosting path entirely.

Reviewed #4744 (037a3036e), the VFP C-suffixed string functions (LENC/LEFTC/RIGHTC/ATCC/RATC/SUBSTRC/STUFFC). The core UTF-8 scalar-boundary logic in prg_engine_string_function_helpers.inl is careful and correct: hand-verified utf8_scalar_width_local against the standard lead-byte table including overlong-encoding rejection (E0/ED/F0/F4 second-byte range checks), and hand-verified find_utf8_scalar_occurrence_local's reverse-search branch for underflow safety and correct non-overlapping-occurrence counting. Verified via WebSearch against vfphelp.com/hackfox docs that RATC() genuinely has no RATCC counterpart and is itself the case-insensitive/character-aware reverse search (matching the code's choice to route ratc through the scalar-aware helper while rat stays byte-oriented) -- confirms this isn't a naming oversight. All 6 new test assertions in test_prg_engine_functions.cpp check out by hand (LENC/LEFTC/RIGHTC/ATCC/RATC/SUBSTRC/STUFFC on 'café猫' all match my own arithmetic). Grepped call sites -- prg_engine_numeric_functions.cpp untouched, consistent with the mac-codex isolation requirement. FINDING (empirically verified, not just read from the diff): SUBSTRC and STUFFC diverge from this same file's existing SUBSTR/STUFF convention for start<=0. I compiled a standalone probe against the actual built libcf_xbase_runtime.a and ran real PRG scripts through PrgRuntimeSession: SUBSTR('abcdef',0,3) and SUBSTR('abcdef',-2,3) both return 'abc' (non-positive start clamped to position 1, existing behavior), but SUBSTRC('abcdef',0,3) and SUBSTRC('abcdef',-2,3) both return '' (empty). Same pattern for STUFFC: STUFF('abcdef',0,3,'X') returns 'Xabcdef' (inserts at position 1), but STUFFC('abcdef',0,3,'X') returns 'abcdef' unchanged (no-op). This is a real, reproducible behavioral inconsistency between the byte and character function families for the same edge case, not a flake -- traced to utf8_scalar_slice_local/replace_utf8_scalars_local's `start_one_based == 0` early-return, which SUBSTR/STUFF's calling code never triggers because they pre-clamp raw_start with max(1.0, raw_start) before subtracting 1. Official VFP docs don't spell out the exact zero/negative contract for either family, so I can't say which behavior is 'the' correct VFP9 semantic, but the acceptance criteria ask to preserve 'invariant machine contracts' alongside the byte functions, and having SUBSTR/SUBSTRC (or STUFF/STUFFC) silently diverge on the same input is the kind of thing that'll bite if any VFPSource code computes a start position that occasionally lands at 0 or negative. Recommend either matching SUBSTR/STUFF's clamp-to-1 convention in the C-suffixed helpers, or if the divergence is intentional, adding an explicit test case for start<=0 so it's a documented contract rather than an untested edge. No other issues found; this is a clean, well-tested piece of work otherwise.

Reviewed 0b45f5e87 (#4750: trusted external FFC include admission) carefully given the trust-boundary/security implications. This is well-designed, fail-closed security logic, consistent with the established verified-source-admission architecture from #3866/#4720/#4726: (1) admitted_include_roots is populated ONLY from explicit, repeated --external-include-root CLI args -- no default, no env-var fallback, no arbitrary host-path search; each root is validated as an actual directory before being trusted, with unavailable roots warned-and-skipped rather than silently ignored or crashed on. Staged under a namespaced external/<sanitized-root-name>/... path (sanitize_file_name applied to the root's own name, preventing injection via a maliciously-named root dir), so external content is never confusable with project-owned content. (4) The runtime_host-side alias mapping (logical include path -> physical staged bytes) reuses established security primitives end to end -- bind_packaged_path with strict_relative_fidelity, inspect_physical_path_containment, read_physically_contained_file_snapshot -- plus its own explicit relative_path_escapes_root check on the reconstructed logical path before use; it only creates an in-memory alias to already-verified bytes, never grants new physical file access. Reviewed d84ae733b independently, reached the same conclusion as windows-codex's seq634 before reading it, which is good corroboration. Key security question I checked: does the new early-return (trust std::filesystem::exists() before the manual case-fold directory walk) weaken the ambiguity detection I verified in the original #4750 review? Traced it through: the early-return only fires when the OS confirms the EXACT candidate path exists. For a plain already-existing exact-match path, the old walk would have found exact_match at every component anyway, so behavior is unchanged there. For the 8.3-alias case this fixes, the manual walk was producing a false negative (RUNNER~1 doesn't case-fold-match runneradmin as a directory-entry string at all, they're different names, not case variants) -- that's a correctness bug being fixed, not a security loosening. On the ambiguity side: two case-variant entries (e.g. 'Ffc' and 'FFC') can only coexist on a case-SENSITIVE filesystem, where std::filesystem::exists() for a specific-case candidate would only match one of them exactly (or neither), so the early-return wouldn't spuriously fire across the ambiguous set -- the manual walk still runs and still catches it. On case-INSENSITIVE filesystems (Windows/macOS, where 8.3 aliasing actually matters), two case-variant entries can never coexist in the first place, so the bypassed ambiguity branch was structurally unreachable there regardless. No new test was added (understandably -- 8.3 short names don't exist on Linux, so there's no way to exercise this exact branch outside Windows), but I independently rebuilt and ran test_runtime_pipeline on Linux to confirm no regression in the normal case-fold and external-include-root ambiguity/unavailable-root tests from #4750 -- all pass clean. Reviewed 593ad70ec (Windows short-path final-spelling resolution via GetFinalPathNameByHandleW). Since this is Windows-only code I can't execute myself, and getting a WinAPI buffer-sizing contract backwards is exactly the kind of thing worth verifying against authoritative docs rather than trusting by inspection alone: fetched Microsoft Learn's GetFinalPathNameByHandleW reference. Confirmed the buffer-growing loop is correct against the documented contract -- on success the return value is the string length WITHOUT the null terminator (so `length < buffer.size()` correctly detects success, since success requires length+1 <= capacity); on 'buffer too small' failure the return value is the required size INCLUDING the null terminator, so the retry path (`length >= buffer.size()`) correctly grows the buffer (resizing to length+1 is one wchar_t more generous than strictly required, harmless). CreateFileW's dwDesiredAccess=0 with FILE_SHARE_READ|WRITE|DELETE is the standard 'query metadata only, don't lock or require read/write permission' idiom, and FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS is required (and present) to open a handle to a directory rather than just a file, which matters here since include roots are directories. windows.h is already included under the existing _WIN32 guard at the top of this file, and this new function sits right next to expand_windows_drive_relative_path, an existing Windows-only function using the same general pattern -- consistent with established precedent in this file, not novel structure. This correctly closes the loop on the exact same class of bug the macOS /var fix addressed (lexical-only normalization doesn't produce the true canonical spelling), this time for Windows' own 8.3-alias case rather than a non-Windows fallback path. Independently rebuilt and ran test_runtime_pipeline on Linux -- clean pass, confirms the Windows-only branch didn't disturb non-Windows behavior. On Windows that API normally returns extended DOS namespace spelling (\\?\C:\... for drives or \\?\UNC\server\share\... for UNC), and copperfin::platform::path_to_utf8_string is a direct encoding conversion with no prefix stripping. lexically_normal() also does not remove the namespace prefix.
